HOA / CC&R DISCLOSURE (DAVIS-STIRLING COMMON INTEREST DEVELOPMENT DISCLOSURE)
Prepared for Pat Morgan · Jordan Lee

HOA/CC&R DISCLOSURE — INTRODUCTION
This HOA/CC&R Disclosure is provided in connection with the sale of 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 by Pat Morgan to Jordan Lee. The property is a separate interest in Maple Grove Homeowners Association, a common interest development. This disclosure is furnished under California's Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act and is separate from, and in addition to, any Transfer Disclosure Statement provided elsewhere in connection with this sale.

DOCUMENTS THE SELLER MUST PROVIDE BEFORE TRANSFER
Before the transfer of title to a separate interest in a common interest development, or the execution of a real property sales contract, the owner must provide the prospective purchaser with: a copy of all governing documents (including, if the association is unincorporated, a written statement to that effect); a copy of the association's most recent annual budget report and related financial documents; a true written statement of the association's current regular and special assessments and fees, any assessments or monetary fines against the owner's interest that remain unpaid as of the date of the statement, and related late-charge, interest, and collection-cost information; a copy or summary of any notice of an unresolved alleged violation of the governing documents previously sent to the owner; a copy of the initial list of construction defects provided to association members, unless the matter has since been resolved and the association has complied with the applicable settlement-disclosure requirements; and, if requested by the purchaser, the minutes of the board's regular meetings for the preceding 12 months. The owner must also provide a copy of the association's most recent exterior elevated elements inspection report.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The owner of a separate interest shall provide the following documents to a prospective purchaser of the separate interest, as soon as practicable before the transfer of title or the execution of a real property sales contract, as defined in Section 2985:"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 4525(a), California Civil Code, Davis-Stirling Act, seller's document-disclosure obligation and timing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=4525.)
  "A copy of all governing documents. If the association is not incorporated, this shall include a statement in writing from an authorized representative of the association that the association is not incorporated."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 4525(a)(1), California Civil Code, governing documents (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=4525.)
  "A copy of the most recent documents distributed pursuant to Article 7 (commencing with Section 5300) of Chapter 6."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 4525(a)(3), California Civil Code, most recent annual budget report documents (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=4525.)
  "A true statement in writing obtained from an authorized representative of the association as to the amount of the association's current regular and special assessments and fees, any assessments levied upon the owner's interest in the common interest development that are unpaid on the date of the statement, and any monetary fines or penalties levied upon the owner's interest and unpaid on the date of the statement."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 4525(a)(4), California Civil Code, assessment and unpaid-amount statement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=4525.)
  "A copy or a summary of any notice previously sent to the owner pursuant to Section 5855 that sets forth any alleged violation of the governing documents that remains unresolved at the time of the request."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 4525(a)(5), California Civil Code, unresolved violation notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=4525.)
  "A copy of the report issued pursuant to the most recent inspection conducted pursuant to Section 5551."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 4525(a)(11), California Civil Code, exterior elevated elements inspection report (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=4525.)
  Known gap: The statutory list in Civil Code § 4525(a) has eleven numbered items; the body above summarizes the most transaction-relevant ones and omits two narrower items (an age-restriction statement keyed to Civil Code § 51.3, and a rental/lease-prohibition statement) that only apply if the governing documents contain those specific restrictions. The task assumption that this list includes a general 'statement regarding pending legal claims/litigation involving the HOA' does not hold up against the statutory text as fetched: § 4525(a) requires disclosure of the initial list of construction defects under the association's builder-defect process (§§ 6000, 6100), which is narrower than a general litigation disclosure, but there is no separate line item in § 4525(a) requiring disclosure of the HOA's pending or threatened litigation generally. All six citations below are to subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 4525(a); they are not independent sections corroborating each other. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Davis-Stirling document-disclosure scheme — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA sale; common-interest-development disclosure regimes vary by state.

HOA'S DEADLINE AND FEE FOR PROVIDING REQUESTED DOCUMENTS
Upon a seller's written request, the association must provide copies of the documents listed above within 10 days of the mailing or delivery of the request. The association may charge the seller a fee for the documents, but only a reasonable fee based on the association's actual cost to procure, prepare, reproduce, and deliver them; no additional fee may be charged for electronic delivery instead of a hard copy. The seller must provide the prospective purchaser, at no cost, with any of these documents the seller already has in the seller's possession.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Upon written request, the association shall, within 10 days of the mailing or delivery of the request, provide the owner of a separate interest, or any other recipient authorized by the owner, with a copy of all of the requested documents specified in Section 4525."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 4530(a)(1), California Civil Code, 10-day deadline to provide requested documents (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=4530.)
  "The association may collect a reasonable fee from the seller based upon the association's actual cost for the procurement, preparation, reproduction, and delivery of the documents requested pursuant to this section. An additional fee shall not be charged for the electronic delivery in lieu of a hard copy delivery of the documents requested."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 4530(b)(1), California Civil Code, fee limited to actual cost — no fixed dollar cap (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=4530.)
  "A seller shall provide to the prospective purchaser, at no cost, current copies of any documents specified by Section 4525 that are in the possession of the seller."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 4530(b)(6), California Civil Code, seller must provide documents already in seller's possession at no cost (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=4530.)
  Known gap: The task brief assumed a specific dollar cap on the fee an HOA may charge for compiling these documents. That assumption does not hold up against the statutory text as fetched: Civil Code § 4530(b)(1) authorizes only a 'reasonable fee' tied to the association's actual cost of procurement, preparation, reproduction, and delivery — there is no fixed dollar ceiling in the statute. The three citations below are all to subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 4530; they are not independent sections corroborating each other. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Davis-Stirling document-disclosure scheme — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA sale; common-interest-development disclosure regimes vary by state.

ITEMIZED FEE DISCLOSURE FORM FOR REQUESTED DOCUMENTS
When the association delivers the requested documents, it must also provide a completed copy of the statutory billing-disclosure form, which itemizes each document the seller may be charged for, the Civil Code section requiring it, whether it was included, and the fee charged for it. A seller may request to purchase some or all of the listed documents but cannot be required to purchase all of them.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The form for billing disclosures required by Section 4530 shall be in at least 10-point type and substantially the following form: CHARGES FOR DOCUMENTS PROVIDED AS REQUIRED BY SECTION 4525"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 4528, California Civil Code, billing-disclosure form is an itemized checklist tied to § 4525 documents (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=4528.)
  "Annual budget report or summary, including reserve study Sections 5300 and 4525(a)(3) Assessment and reserve funding disclosure summary Sections 5300 and 4525(a)(4)"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 4528, California Civil Code, 'Assessment and reserve funding disclosure summary' is one line item on the form (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=4528.)
  "The association shall also provide a recipient authorized by the owner of a separate interest with a copy of the completed form specified in Section 4528 at the time the required documents are delivered."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 4530(d), California Civil Code, association must deliver the § 4528 form with the requested documents (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=4530.)
  Known gap: The task brief assumed Civil Code § 4528 creates a distinct, separately defined 'Assessment and Reserve Funding Disclosure Summary' document. That assumption does not hold up against the statutory text as fetched: § 4528 is the template for the itemized billing-disclosure form required by § 4530(d) — an invoice-style checklist of the documents an association may charge for. 'Assessment and reserve funding disclosure summary' appears on that form only as the label of one line item (cross-referencing Sections 5300 and 4525(a)(4)), not as a freestanding document with its own separately defined statutory content. Both citations below are to the same statutory section, Civil Code § 4528; they are not independent sections corroborating each other. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Davis-Stirling document-disclosure scheme — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA sale; common-interest-development disclosure regimes vary by state.

CONSEQUENCE OF A SELLER'S FAILURE TO DISCLOSE
A transfer is not invalidated solely because a party failed to comply with this disclosure article, and title to the transferred property remains valid. A person who willfully violates this article is liable to the purchaser for the purchaser's actual damages, plus a civil penalty of up to five hundred dollars, and the prevailing party in an action to enforce this liability is entitled to reasonable attorney's fees.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any person who willfully violates this article is liable to the purchaser of a separate interest that is subject to this section for actual damages occasioned thereby and, in addition, shall pay a civil penalty in an amount not to exceed five hundred dollars ($500). In an action to enforce this liability, the prevailing party shall be awarded reasonable attorney's fees."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 4540, California Civil Code, willful-violation damages remedy, capped civil penalty, and fee-shifting (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=4540.)
  "Nothing in this article affects the validity of title to real property transferred in violation of this article."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 4545, California Civil Code, a violation does not affect the validity of title — no rescission remedy (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=4545.)
  Known gap: The task brief asked whether § 4525(f) or a nearby subsection creates a buyer's right of rescission for a seller's failure to provide these HOA documents. That assumption does not hold up against the statutory text as fetched: current Civil Code § 4525 has only subsections (a) and (b) — there is no subsection (f). More importantly, the article's own remedy section, Civil Code § 4540, provides only a damages remedy (actual damages, a civil penalty capped at $500, and fee-shifting to the prevailing party) for a willful violation, and the immediately following section, § 4545, expressly states that a violation does not affect the validity of title. Read together, these two sections affirmatively rule out rescission or invalidation of the sale as a remedy under this article — the opposite of what the brief assumed. This is a different remedial structure than the Transfer Disclosure Statement scheme addressed elsewhere in this corpus (Civil Code § 1102.13), which similarly provides only a non-invalidation/actual-damages remedy rather than rescission, for a related but separate disclosure obligation. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Davis-Stirling document-disclosure scheme — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA sale; common-interest-development disclosure regimes vary by state.

THIS DISCLOSURE IS SEPARATE FROM, AND CUMULATIVE WITH, THE TRANSFER DISCLOSURE STATEMENT
The Davis-Stirling document-disclosure obligation applies to the sale of a 'separate interest' in a common interest development, which includes a condominium unit, a lot or parcel in a planned development, an apartment in a community apartment project, or a unit in a stock cooperative. This obligation arises from a different statutory article than the Transfer Disclosure Statement requirement, which applies to transfers of single-family residential property generally. Where a sale involves a separate interest that also qualifies as single-family residential property, both disclosure obligations can apply to the same transaction, and satisfying one does not by itself satisfy the other.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In a condominium project, “separate interest” means a separately owned unit, as specified in Section 4125. (3) In a planned development, “separate interest” means a separately owned lot, parcel, area, or space."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 4185(a), California Civil Code, 'separate interest' includes condominium units and planned-development lots (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=4185.)
  "Except as provided in Section 1102.2, this article applies to any transfer by sale, exchange, real property sales contract as defined in Section 2985, lease with an option to purchase, any other option to purchase, or ground lease coupled with improvements of any single-family residential property."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102(a), California Civil Code, Transfer Disclosure Statement applies to single-family residential property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.)
  Known gap: This clause draws a distinction between two separate California statutory articles cited elsewhere in this corpus (the Transfer Disclosure Statement clauses under Civil Code § 1102 et seq.) and the Davis-Stirling document-disclosure obligation addressed by this document (Civil Code § 4525 et seq.). It does not resolve, for any specific transaction, whether a given common-interest-development unit meets the 'single-family residential property' scope language used in § 1102(a); that scope question is separately flagged, and left unresolved for the same reason, in this corpus's existing Transfer Disclosure Statement Requirement clause. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Davis-Stirling document-disclosure scheme — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA sale; common-interest-development disclosure regimes vary by state.

BUYER'S ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF RECEIPT
Buyer acknowledges receipt of the governing documents, financial and assessment information, and other documents described in this HOA/CC&R Disclosure for Maple Grove Homeowners Association, including a statement of the association's current regular assessment of $350 per month, before the transfer of title to 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814. Seller: Pat Morgan. Buyer: Jordan Lee.
